raw_response:
I’m farming only 3 mu, so I can’t spread myself too thin. This year I’ll keep 2 mu in the usual wheat-maize rotation, because that gives steady grain and feels safer, and I’ll leave 1 mu in cotton to keep some cash income in case grain prices are not good. I’ve done this kind of mix before, and for a small household like mine, with some people working off-farm, it suits the labor situation better. The extension people always talk about balanced fertilization, but on my land I still lean a little on what I’ve seen work: wheat cannot be short of base fertilizer, maize needs a quick start after wheat harvest, and cotton I won’t push too hard because it takes more labor and the return is not always certain.

For wheat, I’ll sow in early October with a common improved variety from the local dealer, put most fertilizer at planting, and then topdress once around jointing if the stand looks decent. Since I have well water, I’ll irrigate about three times if rainfall is normal: once before winter or at overwintering, once at jointing, and once around grain filling if the soil is dry. After wheat harvest in June, I’ll move fast into summer maize on the same 2 mu with minimum tillage, because the turnaround is tight and I don’t have time or money for too much field work. For cotton on the 1 mu, I’ll keep inputs moderate, use local hybrid seed, water a couple of times, and spray only if I really see pests. I need to watch cash, so I’d rather use round, familiar rates than chase the highest yield.
